Which InChI is this?

InChI now handles metal compounds differently. So that you can tell old from new, the start of every InChI and the end of every InChIKey say which rules made it. Organic compounds keep their InChI and InChIKey.

What changes for you

  • Organic compounds: nothing. Ethanol is still InChI=1S/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3, key LFQSCWFLJHTTHZ-UHFFFAOYSA-N.
  • Any compound with a metal atom: the InChI starts InChI=1BB/ and the InChIKey ends …BB-x. The layers often change too: metal–ligand bonds are now kept instead of cut.
  • Non-standard InChIs (made with options such as -FixedH) start InChI=1N/ instead of InChI=1/.
  • InChI software 1.07 and older cannot read the new prefixes correctly (see below).

Reading the prefix

After InChI=1 come one or two letters. The first says how the InChI was calculated: S standard, B beta (experimental feature), N non-standard options. A second letter B means the Molecular Inorganics rules were used. The InChIKey repeats both letters at positions 24 and 25, with A for "no second letter".

PrefixCalculationRulesInChIKeyExample
InChI=1S/standardbase InChI 1…SA-…ethanol, default options: InChI=1S/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3
InChI=1SB/standardMolecular Inorganics…SB-…not made in this release (Molecular Inorganics is beta)
InChI=1B/betabase InChI 1…BA-…ethanol, -EnhancedStereochemistry: InChI=1B/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3
InChI=1BB/betaMolecular Inorganics…BB-…NaCl, default options: InChI=1BB/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1
InChI=1N/non-standardbase InChI 1…NA-…ethanol, -FixedH: InChI=1N/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3
InChI=1NB/non-standardMolecular Inorganics…NB-…NaCl, -FixedH: InChI=1NB/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1/fCl.Na/h1h;/q-1;m

The second B stands for Molecular Inorganics. Later features are to get C, D, …; how they combine is not decided yet.

Metal compounds

Cisplatin, drawn with its two ammonia ligands bonded to platinum. The old InChI cut every bond to the metal; the new one keeps them. Prefix and key change with it.

Cisplatin

before: InChI=1S/2ClH.2H3N.Pt/h2*1H;2*1H3;/q;;;;+2/p-2
LXZZYRPGZAFOLE-UHFFFAOYSA-L
now: InChI=1BB/Cl2H6N2Pt/c1-5(2,3)4/h3-4H3
NKTISDOLGLLLMZ-UHFFFAOYBB-N

Sodium chloride gives the same layers as before. It still gets the new prefix: the letters say which rules were applied, not whether the result differs.

Sodium chloride

before: InChI=1S/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1
FAPWRFPIFSIZLT-UHFFFAOYSA-M
now: InChI=1BB/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1
FAPWRFPIFSIZLT-UHFFFAOYBB-M

The first 23 letters of the key are the same; only the version letters differ.

One metal atom marks the whole InChI. Ethanol with sodium chloride in one drawing: InChI=1BB/C2H6O.ClH.Na/c1-2-3;;/h3H,2H2,1H3;1H;/q;;+1/p-1.

Borderline elements

Which elements count as metals comes from the Molecular Inorganics element table. Antimony counts; arsenic, germanium and tellurium do not. This is the choice for the beta release; the InChI working group will decide the final list.

CompoundCounted as metalInChI now
SbCl3yesInChI=1BB/Cl3Sb/c1-4(2)3
AsCl3noInChI=1S/AsCl3/c2-1(3)4
GeCl4noInChI=1S/Cl4Ge/c1-5(2,3)4
TeCl4noInChI=1S/Cl4Te/c1-5(2,3)4

Non-standard InChI and the old metal rules

A non-standard InChI now says so with an N. Ethanol with -FixedH: before InChI=1/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3, now InChI=1N/C2H6O/c1-2-3/h3H,2H2,1H3. Old strings starting InChI=1/ are still read and written back as InChI=1N/.

Need the old handling of metals, e.g. to match an existing database? The option -LegacyMetalHandling gives it, marked non-standard. Cisplatin: InChI=1N/2ClH.2H3N.Pt/h2*1H;2*1H3;/q;;;;+2/p-2, key LXZZYRPGZAFOLE-UHFFFAOYNA-L.

Old software

InChI 1.07 and older do not know the new letters. Asked to convert a new InChI, the old program neither refuses nor warns; it drops both letters:

in: InChI=1BB/Cl2H6N2Pt/c1-5(2,3)4/h3-4H3
out: InChI=1/Cl2H6N2Pt/c1-5(2,3)4/h3-4H3

The result reads as an ordinary non-standard InChI. Use current InChI software for strings that start 1BB, 1NB, 1SB or 1N.

Still open

  • How the letters combine when a later feature (C, …) and Molecular Inorganics apply to the same compound.
  • Whether metalloids such as As, Ge, Te (and Sb) count as metals.
  • A table, in the release notes, of what each letter stands for. Some argue against letters altogether.

Your view counts: use the Comment buttons on this page or the general discussion below.

How to use it

No option needed. The new prefixes and InChIKey flags come with InChI 2026.x. For sodium chloride:

$ inchi-1 nacl.mol -STDIO -AuxNone -Key
InChI=1BB/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1
InChIKey=FAPWRFPIFSIZLT-UHFFFAOYBB-M
Warning (Proton(s) added/removed)   (log)

The old metal rules. To reproduce identifiers made by older versions, e.g. to match an existing database, add -LegacyMetalHandling. The result is a non-standard InChI:

$ inchi-1 nacl.mol -STDIO -AuxNone -Key -LegacyMetalHandling
InChI=1N/ClH.Na/h1H;/q;+1/p-1
InChIKey=FAPWRFPIFSIZLT-UHFFFAOYNA-M
Warning (Proton(s) added/removed)   (log)

Reading. InChI 2026.x reads all prefixes, including the old InChI=1/, which it writes back as InChI=1N/. Software built on InChI 1.07 or older cannot read the new prefixes (see above).

Every InChI and InChIKey on this page is computed by InChI (dev, before and after PR #280), not typed in. Issue: IUPAC-InChI/InChI #285. Full rules: specification Versioning of InChI and InChIKey. More examples, old vs. new: comparison table. All features: InChI Specifications.
